part4.spec: Write one original 300–400 word academic monologue in British English for a non-specialist audience, using only speaker A. lines.text:
Today we'll consider how archivists protect paper documents from damage. An archive is a collection kept for long-term use, but it also refers to the organisation responsible for that collection. Our concern is not the contents of any one letter. Instead, we'll examine the conditions that help a collection survive, and the practical decisions that staff must make when resources are limited.

First, let's look at the storage environment. Fluctuating humidity can cause paper to expand and contract repeatedly. This movement places stress on the material, so staff use a monitor to record humidity rather than relying on how the room feels. Temperature matters as well, but a reading taken once does not describe conditions over an entire year. Regular records allow staff to identify a persistent problem and assess whether an intervention has made a difference.

Next, consider light. Exposure can fade inks, and the effect accumulates over time. Consequently, documents not currently being consulted are kept in boxes. These provide a physical barrier against light as well as dust. A box should fit its contents: forcing a large document into a small container can cause folds or tears. Labels on the outside reduce the need to open several boxes when retrieving a particular item.

The third aspect is handling. Readers may need to consult a document directly, but staff can support fragile sheets on a board when moving them. A board spreads the load and reduces bending. Staff should also keep food away from the consultation area, since crumbs may attract insects. If a document is torn, an unsuitable adhesive can make later treatment more difficult, so repairs should be referred to a trained conservator.

Finally, remember that copying is not a substitute for storing an original safely. A digital copy can reduce handling and increase access, but the copy itself requires secure storage and periodic checking. The general principle is to combine suitable environmental conditions, protective containers and careful handling, while recording what is done so that later staff can review those decisions.

part3.spec: Write one original IELTS Academic Part 3 educational discussion in British English, in a natural spoken register, between a student and a tutor or two students. Use 300–400 words and alternate A and B. Choose a plausible project, presentation or research assignment. Set exactly five four-option questions in listening order: three about details or reasons, one about an explicitly expressed attitude or reservation, and one requiring the two correct statements from five named candidate statements A–E. For the last question give four different pairs as the four options; exactly one pair must be fully supported. Test the supplied detail, stance and evidence points. Build distractors from alternatives, rejected proposals, different speakers or conditions in the conversation; do not rely on intonation. Write explanations in Chinese and identify the spoken evidence. Do not include living people, news, or claims requiring specialist knowledge.

lines.text: I've brought the outline for my project on the campus gardens. I originally planned to compare all four gardens, but after walking around them I realised that two are closed for repairs. So I will concentrate on the remaining pair instead.

That sounds manageable. What exactly will you compare? Remember that a project needs a question you can answer with the time and equipment available, rather than a general description of everything you see.

I'd like to compare the number of different insects visiting the flower beds. I thought of counting birds too, but that would require a separate observation schedule, and I only have three weeks for fieldwork.
Fine. Your outline suggests taking photographs at midday. Why choose that time? The gardens are open throughout the day, so you should explain why a narrower period helps your comparison.
It's mainly because both gardens receive direct sunlight then. If I visited one in shade and one in sun, that difference might affect what I see. I can also make all my visits between twelve and one.

Consistency is useful, though it won't tell you what happens at other hours. You should acknowledge that limitation when you present your findings. What do you think about asking volunteers to identify the insects from your photographs?

I agree that volunteers could help with the volume of images. However, I'm concerned that inexperienced people might confuse similar species. I'd only use their classifications if someone with relevant training checked them afterwards.

That's a reasonable condition. Before you start, obtain permission from the garden manager and test the camera in both locations. You mentioned buying a new lens, but try the department's equipment first. And you don't need to interview visitors or collect any plants for this question.

I'll contact the manager this afternoon and arrange the camera test for Friday. Then I can revise the timetable if the images are not clear enough. I'll also include the limitation about the time of day in my report.
Good. Bring a short record of the trial next week, including the weather and where you stood. That will help us decide whether the method is practical before the observations begin.

lines.text: Good morning. I would like to register for one of the weekend pottery courses advertised at the community centre. Could you tell me a little about the arrangements before I give you my details?
Of course. We have a beginner group on Saturdays and another on Sundays. Both meet in the same studio, and all the basic equipment is included in the course fee.
The Saturday group would suit me. I first thought I could start on the twelfth, but I have an appointment that morning. Is there still a place for the nineteenth?
Yes, there is one place left on the nineteenth. I'll put that date down. May I take your surname, please?
It is Merrin, spelled M E double R I N. My sister has a different spelling, so I always make sure people have the right one.
Thank you. And which street do you live on? We send the joining information by post as well as by email, because it includes a map of the building.
I live on Willow Street. There is also a Willow Road across town, so please make sure you write Street. My house number is fourteen.
I've got that. The course costs eighty pounds in total, including materials. We ask for a deposit of twenty pounds when you book; the rest is due on the first day.
That is fine. Is there anything I should bring? I have an apron at home, but I do not own any tools. I would prefer not to buy equipment until I know whether I enjoy the course.
An apron is useful, and please bring a towel as well. We provide the tools. Your class starts at ten, and reception opens half an hour earlier. I'll send your confirmation today.

groups.text:
Passage 1: Comparing Shade

P1
A town study examined shade at two public squares during summer. groups.text:
Should Museum Visitors Be Allowed to Touch?

For most of the twentieth century, the rule in museum galleries was simple: look, but do not touch. Glass cases, rope barriers and printed notices all communicated the same message. In recent decades, however, many museums have introduced handling sessions in which visitors may pick up selected objects under supervision. Some commentators regard this as a welcome change in attitude; others see it as a risk that institutions responsible for irreplaceable material should not accept. In my view, both positions contain something true, but neither should be adopted without qualification.

The case for handling is usually made by education staff. They argue that touch provides information that sight alone cannot: the weight of a tool, the texture of a woven cloth or the balance of a pot in the hand. A visitor who lifts an iron cooking pot, they say, understands the labour of preparing a meal in a way that no label can convey. I find this argument persuasive, at least for objects whose use depended on the human body. It is difficult to appreciate a heavy tool from behind glass, and a short period of handling can make a description in a guidebook far easier to understand.

Conservators, whose task is to preserve collections, raise a different concern. Human skin carries oils and salts, and repeated contact can mark metal, stain textiles and weaken painted surfaces. Accidental drops are a further risk. Some conservators have argued that every touch shortens an object's life, however careful the visitor may be. This claim is sometimes dismissed as excessive caution, but I think it deserves to be taken seriously. Damage caused by handling is gradual, and it may not become visible until long after the decision to allow contact has been forgotten.

The solution adopted by many museums is a separate handling collection. This consists of objects that are not unique: duplicates of items already well represented in the main collection, replicas made for the purpose, or items whose historical value lies in their type rather than in their individual history. I regard this as the most sensible arrangement currently available. It allows visitors to experience weight and texture while ensuring that the objects most important to research are not exposed to repeated contact. It is sometimes objected that a replica cannot give the experience of touching something genuinely old. That is true, but the objection overlooks the fact that many duplicates in handling collections are themselves genuine.

There remains the question of who should benefit. Handling sessions are often arranged for school groups, and adult visitors may never be offered the opportunity. Museum managers sometimes explain that children gain more from physical activity than adults do. I am not convinced by this reasoning. Adults also learn through their hands, and a retired engineer or a practising weaver may notice features of an object that a curator would miss. Limiting handling to children therefore reduces the range of knowledge that the sessions could produce.

It should also be recognised that handling is not the only way to bring visitors closer to objects. Detailed photographs, models that can be taken apart and recordings of specialists demonstrating a technique may answer some of the questions that touch would answer. These methods do not replace physical contact, but they can extend something of its value to objects that could never safely be handled. A museum that offers only one of these approaches is, in my opinion, making less of its collection than it could.

Finally, the success of handling depends on supervision. A session led by a trained member of staff can teach visitors how to hold an object correctly, and this knowledge may make them more careful elsewhere in the museum. Without such guidance, handling is little more than permission to pick things up. The question is therefore not simply whether visitors should touch, but under what conditions, with which objects and with what help. Answered in that way, it becomes a question that museums can resolve rather than an argument between two fixed positions.

Keeping Seeds for the Future

A. Many plant species are under pressure from changes in land use, the spread of disease and shifts in climate. When a species disappears from the wild, its genetic material is lost with it, and no later effort can recover it. Seed banks were established as a form of insurance against such losses. By holding samples of seeds from many populations, they aim to ensure that material remains available for research and, if necessary, for returning plants to places where they have died out. A seed bank does not prevent a species from declining, but it can preserve options that would otherwise disappear. For this reason, collectors often concentrate on plants that are rare, plants found only in a small area and plants with uses in farming or medicine. Wild relatives of crops receive particular attention, since they may carry characteristics that breeders could one day need.

B. The method used for most seeds is straightforward in principle. After collection, the seeds are cleaned and examined so that empty or damaged ones can be removed. They are then dried slowly in a room with low humidity until only a small proportion of their weight is water. Drying is essential, because water inside a seed would form ice crystals when frozen and damage its cells. Once dried, the seeds are sealed in airtight containers and placed in cold storage, usually at around minus twenty degrees Celsius. Under these conditions, the chemical processes that cause seeds to age are slowed dramatically, and many species can remain alive for decades or longer. The freezers themselves are monitored constantly, since a failure in temperature control could affect thousands of samples at once.

C. Storage alone, however, does not guarantee that a collection remains useful. A seed that looks perfect may no longer be able to grow. Seed banks therefore take a small number of seeds from each sample at regular intervals and try to germinate them under suitable conditions of light, warmth and moisture. If the proportion that sprouts begins to fall, staff know that the sample is deteriorating. Samples that pass the test are returned to the freezer, and the date and result of each test are recorded. Where results are poor, staff can grow plants from the remaining seeds and collect fresh seed from them before the stored sample loses its value. These tests use up seeds, so collectors try to gather enough at the outset to allow for many years of checking. The results also help researchers to estimate how long the seeds of different species can be kept.

D. Not every plant produces seeds that can be treated in this way. Some species have seeds that die if they lose too much water, so they cannot be dried before freezing. These are known as recalcitrant seeds. The acorns of oak trees are a familiar example, and the group also includes many trees of tropical forests, where seeds often germinate soon after they fall. For such species, seed banks must use other methods. Small pieces of the embryo may be removed and stored in liquid nitrogen at far lower temperatures, or plants may be kept growing in living collections. These approaches are more demanding than drying and freezing, and they are not yet available for every species that needs them.

E. Even a large and well-managed seed bank cannot do the work of protecting plants where they grow. A stored sample represents the genetic variety of a population at the moment it was collected. In the wild, populations continue to adapt to changing conditions, interacting with the insects that pollinate them and with the soils and climates around them. A sample kept frozen for fifty years has not experienced the changes of those fifty years. Seeds can be returned to restore habitats, but only if suitable habitats still exist to receive them. For this reason, those who manage seed banks generally describe their work as one part of conservation rather than an alternative to it. Their collections are most valuable when they support efforts to keep natural populations healthy.

Lights on the Coast

[A] For as long as ships have sailed close to land, coastlines have been among the most dangerous parts of any voyage. Rocks, sandbanks and headlands that are easy to avoid in daylight become serious hazards at night or in poor weather. Lighthouses were built to mark such dangers and to guide vessels safely into harbours. Some stood on headlands, while others were built on isolated rocks far from the shore, where construction itself was extremely difficult. A light on the shore told a navigator two things at once: that land was near, and roughly where the danger lay. In the busiest waters, a chain of lights along the coast allowed ships to pass from one to the next through the night.

[B] The earliest lights were simply fires. Wood or coal was burned in an iron basket at the top of a tower or on a high point of land. Such fires had obvious weaknesses. They consumed great quantities of fuel, they were difficult to keep burning in wind and rain, and the light they gave was scattered in every direction, including upwards and inland, where it was of no use to sailors. All the fuel had to be carried up to the fire by hand. Enclosed oil lamps placed behind glass, which came into use later, were far more dependable than open fires in bad weather, although a single flame on its own still gave only a weak light at a distance.

[C] The most important improvement came in the 1820s with a new kind of lens designed by the French engineer Augustin Fresnel. Instead of one thick piece of glass, his lens was made of rings of glass prisms arranged around a central lens. Each ring bent the light from the lamp so that, instead of spreading out, it travelled in a narrow, concentrated beam towards the horizon. Because it used far less glass than a solid lens of the same size, it was lighter and absorbed less of the light passing through it. A lamp fitted with such a lens could be seen many kilometres further out to sea.

[D] A light is only useful if sailors know which light they are looking at. For this reason, each lighthouse was given its own pattern, known as its character. One light might show a single flash every five seconds, while another nearby might give two flashes every fifteen seconds or show a steady light with a red section visible from one direction. These patterns were printed in lists and on charts, so a navigator who timed the flashes with a watch could identify the lighthouse and work out the ship's position. Some lights also used colour to warn ships that they were approaching from a dangerous direction.

[E] For more than a century, every major lighthouse needed people living beside it. The keepers trimmed the wicks, refilled the oil, cleaned soot from the glass and, in many towers, wound the clockwork that turned the lens through the night. They recorded weather and passing ships in a logbook. During the twentieth century, electric lamps, automatic switches and remote monitoring gradually removed the need for these tasks to be done on site. Once a light could be checked and controlled from a distant office, resident keepers were withdrawn, and by the end of the century the last of them in Britain had left their posts.

[F] Today most ships carry satellite navigation systems that can show their position at any moment, and some people have asked whether lighthouses are still required. The authorities responsible for them have kept many lights in service, arguing that electronic equipment can fail and that a visible light provides an independent check that does not depend on power supplies on board. At some stations the old lens has been removed and replaced by a smaller modern light, which needs far less maintenance. Lights that are no longer needed for navigation have sometimes been sold, and a number have become museums, holiday homes or places from which to observe seabirds and marine mammals.

groups.text:
How Bridges Carry Their Loads

Every bridge has to solve the same basic problem: it must carry its own weight and the weight of whatever crosses it, and pass those forces safely to the ground. Engineers have developed several distinct ways of doing this. The choice between them depends on the distance to be crossed, the ground at each side, the materials available and the cost. Five common types illustrate the range of solutions.

The simplest is the beam bridge. In its most basic form, it is a horizontal beam resting on a support at each end, like a plank laid across a stream. When a load crosses, the beam bends slightly: its upper part is squeezed while its lower part is stretched. Because the beam has to resist this bending along its whole length, its depth must increase as the span grows, and the bridge quickly becomes heavy. For this reason, beam bridges are generally used for relatively short crossings, although a long distance can be covered by a series of beams resting on many intermediate supports, as on many road viaducts.

An arch bridge works in a different way. Its curved shape turns the downward force of a load into pressure that travels around the curve and out into the ground at each end. The material of the arch is therefore mostly squeezed rather than bent, which is why stone, a material that is strong under pressure but weak when stretched, was so widely used for arches. The ground at the ends must be firm enough to resist the outward push; otherwise the arch may spread and collapse. Many arch bridges built centuries ago remain in use, a sign of how well this form suits masonry.

For the longest spans, engineers have usually chosen the suspension bridge. Its deck hangs from vertical cables attached to two main cables, and these main cables pass over the tops of tall towers before being fixed into massive anchorages in the ground at each end. The main cables are in tension, pulled tight by the weight they carry. Because steel cable is very strong for its weight, this arrangement allows a deck to stretch well over a kilometre between towers. Its weakness is a tendency to move in strong winds, which designers counter by making the deck stiff or giving it a shape that air flows past smoothly.

A cantilever is a structure fixed at one end and free at the other, like a diving board. A cantilever bridge uses pairs of such arms projecting from piers towards each other, sometimes with a short section suspended between their tips. One practical advantage of this design lies in the way it can be built. Because each arm is supported by its own pier, it can be extended outwards piece by piece without any temporary structure underneath. This made the design useful over deep water or busy shipping channels, where scaffolding from below would be impractical.

Cable-stayed bridges look similar to suspension bridges from a distance, since both use towers and cables. The difference lies in how the cables are arranged. In a cable-stayed bridge, the cables run in straight lines directly from each tower to points along the deck, and the pull of the cables on one side of a tower balances the pull on the other. Unlike a suspension bridge, therefore, it needs no heavy anchorages at the ends of the bridge. The former, by contrast, depends on its anchorages to keep the main cables tight. The cable-stayed design has become common for medium and long spans in recent decades, partly because it can be built relatively quickly and uses less cable.

None of these types is better than the others in every situation. A short rural crossing may need nothing more than a beam, while a wide estuary may require a suspension or cable-stayed design. In practice, engineers often combine features, for example by using a series of beams for the approaches to a larger central span. Understanding how each type carries its load helps to explain why bridges in different places look so different.

Roofs That Grow

In most towns, roofs are among the largest surfaces exposed to the weather, yet they are rarely designed to do more than keep rain out. A green roof is one covered with a layer of growing plants. The idea is not new: roofs covered with turf have been used on houses in parts of northern Europe for centuries. Modern green roofs, however, are built in layers that allow plants to grow on top of a building without damaging the structure underneath. In some cities, green roofs are now encouraged on new buildings, particularly in areas where the drains are already under pressure.

The lowest layer is a waterproof membrane, which protects the roof itself, just as it would on an ordinary flat roof. Above this lies a root barrier. Plant roots search for water and can force their way into small cracks, so the barrier is needed to stop them from reaching and piercing the membrane. Next comes a drainage layer, often made of plastic sheets shaped with small cups or channels, which holds a little water for the plants and lets the rest flow away towards the roof's outlets. On top of the drainage layer is a filter fabric. Its job is to stop fine particles of soil from being washed downwards, where they would gradually block the drainage layer. Finally there is the growing medium, usually a mixture lighter than ordinary garden soil, in which the plants are set.

Green roofs are generally divided into two kinds. Extensive green roofs have a thin growing layer, often less than fifteen centimetres deep, planted with low, hardy species such as sedums that can survive long periods without rain. Once the plants are established, these roofs need little maintenance beyond an occasional inspection and the removal of unwanted seedlings. They add relatively little weight and can often be placed on existing buildings. Intensive green roofs, by contrast, have much deeper soil and can support lawns, shrubs and even small trees. They are often designed to be used like gardens, but they need regular watering and care, and their weight means that the building beneath must be considerably stronger. On either kind of roof, the plants have to be chosen to suit the depth of soil available.

One of the main reasons for building green roofs is the way they handle rain. During a storm, an ordinary roof sends water straight into the drains, and in towns where most surfaces are hard, the drains can be overwhelmed. A green roof holds part of the rain in its growing medium and plants, and releases the rest more slowly. This reduces the amount of water reaching the drains at the height of a storm. There is, however, a limit. Once the growing medium is saturated, further rain runs off much as it would from any other roof, so the benefit is greatest during moderate storms rather than during long periods of heavy rain.

Green roofs also affect temperature. The plants and growing medium insulate the building beneath, reducing the loss of heat in winter. The effect is greatest on buildings with large flat roofs and little insulation of their own. In summer, water evaporating from the leaves helps to keep the roof surface cooler than bare materials, which absorb the sun's heat. Across a whole district, a large number of green roofs might help to reduce the extra warmth that builds up in cities, but a single roof on its own makes very little difference to the temperature of the surrounding streets.

Green roofs can also provide habitats for insects and birds, though these are small, exposed and often separated from other green spaces. Some are sown with a mixture of local wild flowers to attract bees and butterflies. Against these benefits must be set the costs. A green roof is more expensive to install than a conventional one, and an existing building must be assessed by an engineer before any extra weight is added. As with many such measures, the advantages depend less on the idea itself than on careful design for a particular building.

How Sand Dunes Grow

Sand dunes form along coasts where there is a plentiful supply of sand and a strong onshore wind. At low tide, large areas of beach are exposed to the air. As the surface dries, the wind picks up loose grains and carries them inland, bouncing them along the ground. The grains are light enough to be moved easily but too heavy to be lifted high into the air. When the moving sand meets an obstacle, such as a line of seaweed, a piece of driftwood or a small plant, the wind slows down and drops some of its load. A small heap of sand builds up on the sheltered side of the obstacle, and if conditions remain favourable, the heap continues to grow.

These first low mounds, known as embryo dunes, are fragile. They lie close to the sea and may be washed away by a high tide or a storm. A few plants are able to survive here, tolerating salt spray and occasional flooding by sea water. Their stems and leaves slow the wind further and trap more sand, so that the dune gradually rises above the reach of most tides.

Once a dune has grown a little higher, a different plant takes over. Marram grass is particularly well suited to life on young dunes. Most plants are harmed if they are covered by sand, but marram grows more vigorously when it is buried, pushing new shoots upwards through each fresh layer. As it does so, the dune grows with it, and dunes dominated by marram can reach a considerable height. Below the surface, the plant spreads by means of long roots and underground stems, which form a dense network that holds the loose sand together. Marram is also adapted to the dry conditions of an exposed dune. In dry weather, its leaves roll inwards, which reduces the area from which water is lost and protects the pores through which the plant breathes.

As dunes become more stable, they change in character. Plants that die and decay add organic matter to the sand, which begins to hold water and nutrients. A wider range of species can then grow, including mosses, lichens and low flowering plants. These older dunes, further from the sea, often look grey rather than yellow because of the cover of mosses and lichens, and the marram that built them becomes less common, since it no longer receives the fresh sand it needs to thrive. Further inland still, the oldest dunes may eventually be colonised by shrubs and trees.

Dunes are valuable to people as well as to wildlife. They act as a natural barrier between the sea and the land behind, absorbing the energy of storm waves and supplying sand to beaches that have been eroded. In some places they also protect farmland and buildings from flooding by the sea. They are also popular places for walking and recreation, and this can create problems. Where people walk repeatedly along the same route, the plants are crushed and eventually die. Without roots to hold it, the sand is exposed to the wind, which may scoop out a deep hollow in the side of the dune, known as a blowout. Once formed, a blowout can grow rapidly and may cut right through the dune.

Coastal managers use several methods to repair such damage. One is to put up fences made of brushwood, which slow the wind and cause it to drop sand on the damaged area, much as a natural obstacle would. Another is to plant marram grass by hand on bare sand, so that its roots can begin to bind the surface again. To prevent further damage, managers often lay boardwalks across the dunes so that visitors keep to fixed routes rather than spreading out over the vegetation. These measures are most successful when combined, and when the supply of sand from the beach remains sufficient for the dunes to keep growing.

Inside a Modern Beehive

For most of history, people who kept honeybees housed them in simple containers. In much of northern Europe, the usual choice was the skep, a dome-shaped basket woven from straw. Bees built their wax combs inside it, fixing them to the walls, and the combs could not be removed without being broken. To collect the honey, beekeepers often had to destroy the combs and sometimes the colony itself. The modern hive, developed in the nineteenth century, solved this problem by giving the bees removable wooden frames on which to build their combs. Its design depends on a simple discovery: bees leave a gap of a particular width, often called the bee space, between combs and the walls around them, and if every space in the hive is of about this width, the bees will not fill it with wax. The frames can therefore be lifted out, inspected and replaced.

A modern hive is built as a stack of boxes, each of which has a particular purpose. At the very bottom is the floor, a flat wooden base on which the rest of the hive stands. Some floors are made of fine mesh, which lets air circulate beneath the colony. Along the front edge of the floor there is a narrow gap, the entrance, through which the bees fly in and out. In cold weather the beekeeper can fit a strip of wood to make the entrance smaller, which helps the colony to defend itself and keep warm.

Directly on top of the floor sits the brood box. This is the deepest box in the hive, and it holds the frames on which the queen lays her eggs. Here the young bees develop, cared for by the workers, and the colony also stores some honey and pollen around the edges of these combs for its own use. The brood box is the heart of the colony, and beekeepers disturb it as little as possible.

Above the brood box lies the queen excluder. It is a flat grid, usually made of metal or plastic, with slots wide enough for worker bees to pass through but too narrow for the queen, whose body is larger. Because the queen cannot climb beyond it, no eggs are laid in the boxes above, and the combs there contain only honey. This makes it possible to harvest honey without removing young bees.

The boxes placed above the excluder are called supers. They are shallower than the brood box, partly because a box full of honey is very heavy and a shallower box is easier to lift. During a good summer, the workers fill the supers with honey, and the beekeeper may add further supers on top as the season goes on. At the end of the season, the supers are removed and the honey is extracted from their combs.

On top of the highest super is the crown board, a flat wooden sheet that covers the stack of boxes. It usually has a small hole in the centre, which can be used to feed the bees or fitted with a device that lets them leave the boxes below but not return. The crown board also means that, when the outermost cover is lifted off, the bees remain inside the boxes rather than flying straight out.

The final part is the roof, which fits over the crown board and keeps rain out of the hive. Roofs are often covered with a sheet of metal on top and are made with deep sides that overlap the boxes below, so that wind cannot lift them easily.

When inspecting a hive, the beekeeper usually uses a smoker, a small metal container in which material such as dry grass is burned to produce cool smoke. A little smoke at the entrance and under the cover makes the bees calmer and less likely to sting. The smoker is not part of the hive itself, but few beekeepers would open a hive without one.

groups.text:
When Every Town Kept Its Own Time

Today it seems obvious that a clock in one part of a country should show the same time as a clock in another. Until the middle of the nineteenth century, however, this was not the case in Britain. Each town kept its own local time, based on the position of the sun. Noon was the moment when the sun stood highest in the sky, and because the sun appears to move from east to west, noon arrived a little later in western towns than in eastern ones. Bristol, for example, kept a time about ten minutes behind that of London.

For most people, these differences hardly mattered. Life was organised around local events, and few people travelled far. Many villages had only one public clock, usually on the church, and it was set by the sun. Even for those who did, the stagecoach was slow enough for the difference to pass almost unnoticed. A journey from London to the west of England took many hours, and coach guards simply adjusted their watches as they went, so that passengers arrived to find the clocks of their destination agreeing with the guard's watch.

The railways changed this situation. Trains covered in a few hours distances that had previously taken a day or more, and they ran to published timetables. A timetable that listed departures in the local time of each station was confusing for passengers, who might find that a train appeared to take less time travelling in one direction than in the other. Passengers who wanted to change trains at another station had to calculate the difference for themselves. More seriously, railway staff working in different towns could be using different times. On lines where trains in both directions shared a single track, a misunderstanding about the time could bring two trains onto the same stretch of line, with obvious danger.

Railway companies therefore began to adopt a single standard. The Great Western Railway is generally recorded as the first, introducing London time on its routes in 1840. Other companies followed, and by the end of the 1840s most British railways had adopted the same practice. The time they used was that of the Royal Observatory at Greenwich, in London, which had long kept accurate time for the purposes of navigation. Railway time, as it was often called, became a familiar idea within a few years.

Keeping clocks in agreement over long distances required a means of sending the time from one place to another. This was provided by the electric telegraph, which was being built alongside many railway lines in the same period. From the 1850s, signals sent from Greenwich could tell stations and post offices across the country the exact time, allowing their clocks to be checked and corrected regularly.

Not every town welcomed the change. Some local authorities saw no reason why their clocks should follow London rather than the sun, and for a time two systems existed side by side. A number of public clocks were made with two minute hands, one showing local time and the other London time. Gradually, however, the convenience of a single time won out, as more and more of daily life came to be organised around trains, post and telegraph.

The question was finally settled by law. In 1880, Parliament passed an act making Greenwich Mean Time the legal time throughout Great Britain. A few years later, at an international conference held in Washington in 1884, delegates chose the meridian passing through Greenwich as the starting point for measuring longitude around the world, a decision that later became the basis of the system of time zones used today.

The story of railway time shows how a change in technology can alter something as basic as the way people measure the day. Local solar time had served communities well for centuries, but once fast travel and instant communication linked distant towns, a shared time became a practical necessity. It is a reminder that standards which now seem natural were once a matter of local debate.

groups.text:
How Sand Dunes Grow

Sand dunes form along coasts where there is a plentiful supply of sand and a strong onshore wind. At low tide, large areas of beach are exposed to the air. As the surface dries, the wind picks up loose grains and carries them inland, bouncing them along the ground. The grains are light enough to be moved easily but too heavy to be lifted high into the air. When the moving sand meets an obstacle, such as a line of seaweed, a piece of driftwood or a small plant, the wind slows down and drops some of its load. A small heap of sand builds up on the sheltered side of the obstacle, and if conditions remain favourable, the heap continues to grow.

These first low mounds, known as embryo dunes, are fragile. They lie close to the sea and may be washed away by a high tide or a storm. A few plants are able to survive here, tolerating salt spray and occasional flooding by sea water. Their stems and leaves slow the wind further and trap more sand, so that the dune gradually rises above the reach of most tides.

Once a dune has grown a little higher, a different plant takes over. Marram grass is particularly well suited to life on young dunes. Most plants are harmed if they are covered by sand, but marram grows more vigorously when it is buried, pushing new shoots upwards through each fresh layer. As it does so, the dune grows with it, and dunes dominated by marram can reach a considerable height. Below the surface, the plant spreads by means of long roots and underground stems, which form a dense network that holds the loose sand together. Marram is also adapted to the dry conditions of an exposed dune. In dry weather, its leaves roll inwards, which reduces the area from which water is lost and protects the pores through which the plant breathes.

As dunes become more stable, they change in character. Plants that die and decay add organic matter to the sand, which begins to hold water and nutrients. A wider range of species can then grow, including mosses, lichens and low flowering plants. These older dunes, further from the sea, often look grey rather than yellow because of the cover of mosses and lichens, and the marram that built them becomes less common, since it no longer receives the fresh sand it needs to thrive. Further inland still, the oldest dunes may eventually be colonised by shrubs and trees.

Dunes are valuable to people as well as to wildlife. They act as a natural barrier between the sea and the land behind, absorbing the energy of storm waves and supplying sand to beaches that have been eroded. In some places they also protect farmland and buildings from flooding by the sea. They are also popular places for walking and recreation, and this can create problems. Where people walk repeatedly along the same route, the plants are crushed and eventually die. Without roots to hold it, the sand is exposed to the wind, which may scoop out a deep hollow in the side of the dune, known as a blowout. Once formed, a blowout can grow rapidly and may cut right through the dune.

Coastal managers use several methods to repair such damage. One is to put up fences made of brushwood, which slow the wind and cause it to drop sand on the damaged area, much as a natural obstacle would. Another is to plant marram grass by hand on bare sand, so that its roots can begin to bind the surface again. To prevent further damage, managers often lay boardwalks across the dunes so that visitors keep to fixed routes rather than spreading out over the vegetation. These measures are most successful when combined, and when the supply of sand from the beach remains sufficient for the dunes to keep growing.
